1:
What the right is that God should hear. gets three answers. Charles Ellicott takes it for justice, notes that some ancient versions read it as a title and others make it concrete, Hear me, the righteous, and judges that the Authorised Version has the true sense. John Gill canvasses more: it may be the righteous cause, or the prayer in righteousness as the Targum has it, or the righteous one himself. C.H. Spurgeon reports a rendering making it the Messiah, adopted by Jerome and admired by Bishop Horsley, and adds that whether or not it is correct as a translation it is proper as a plea.

Why the plea is repeated three times in a single verse draws C.H. Spurgeon into a rebuke. He that has the worst cause makes the most noise, so the oppressed soul fears its voice may be drowned; yet some professors set such small store by the mercy-seat that God does not hear them for the simple reason that they neglect to plead, which is as good as having no house and choosing to live in the lanes. There is more fear, he says, that we will not hear the Lord than that he will not hear us. Matthew Henry supplies the pleas the psalmist makes: that he was sincere, since feigned prayers are fruitless while a heart that leads the prayer is met with favour; and that he had prayed at other times, so that it is a comfort if trouble, when it comes, finds the wheels of prayer already going.

The occasion is placed historically by some and lifted out of history by others. Adam Clarke puts it about the time when Saul had carried his persecution to its highest pitch, records that the Arabic calls it the prayer of a perfect man or of Christ himself, and mentions Delaney’s view that it followed the parting with Jonathan. John Calvin says the inscription fixes no time but that David probably complains of Saul and his associates. Augustine of Hippo assigns the prayer to the Person of the Lord, with the addition of the Church which is his body. Keil and Delitzsch place it by style: it follows its neighbour because it closes with the same hope of a blessed vision of God, and is the first written in what they call the indignant style, where David’s language, elsewhere so flowing and clear, becomes harsh and full of unresolved dissonances as he describes his enemies.

The night trial is where the entry gathers. Keil and Delitzsch take it for the divine testing of the inward parts, a trying of gold by fire; and the result of the scrutiny God made in the night, when the bottom of a man’s heart is made manifest, whether in waking thought or in the fancies of the sleeper, was that he found nothing to punish, nothing separated as dross from the gold. Charles Ellicott calls the night the time of calm reflection and self-examination. John Wesley gives the reason: at night men’s minds, freed from business and from company, act more freely according to their inclinations. Adam Clarke renders the trying as the assaying of metals to detect their alloy, and quotes his old Psalter, which has God examining him in the likeness of the furnace that purges metal, wickedness not being found in him.

The last clause is a crux. Charles Ellicott says the Hebrew presents a difficulty and would take the word as a noun meaning evil counsels, joining it to what precedes rather than what follows, so that the lines run that God found no malice in him and that it does not pass his mouth — an arrangement the ancient versions support. John Wesley keeps the received sense and makes it a resolution taken on deliberation: he is so far from practising against Saul’s life that he will not wrong him in a word.
4:
What the works of men are is settled quickly; the next clause is not. John Gill takes them for the works of wicked men, among whom the psalmist lived, and John Wesley makes the observation the motive: seeing how wicked this age was, he resolved to take more care in ordering his own actions. Charles Ellicott keeps it neutral, as regards the actions of men, and defends the received rendering of the next words against those who would read against the word, since the point is that the divine standard for action, and not the worldly one, governs the writer.

The paths of the destroyer are where the trouble lies. Adam Clarke calls the passage exceedingly obscure and notes that some render the phrase hard or difficult paths; he then gives his old Psalter, which takes it that way and turns it into a warning — the speaker has kept the hard ways of virtue and tribulation, which men think hard, and therefore they leave the hard way to heaven and take the soft way to hell, but that way is full hard at the end. Charles Ellicott finds a difficulty of another kind: the Hebrew says literally that he has observed ways of violence, and usage almost compels us to read that as having kept them, which is impossible here, so that we must either give the verb the unusual sense of guarding against or suppose an error in the text. John Wesley has no such trouble, taking the paths for the customs of the violent man, such as Saul with his courtiers.

Whether the next verse is a prayer or a claim divides the entry sharply. Charles Ellicott says it is not imperative at all, that being opposed to the context, since the psalmist is still asserting his innocence; he renders it that his course kept close in God’s tracks and his footsteps have not wavered, the word for paths meaning wheel-tracks. Everyone else reads a petition. John Gill takes it as showing David conscious of his own weakness and sensible of his need of divine power. Adam Clarke presses further: David walked in God’s ways, but without divine assistance could not walk steadily even in them, and having been kept from the paths of the destroyer was not enough, for he must walk in God’s paths and spend his life in obedience — negative holiness, he says, can save no man.

C.H. Spurgeon works the petition into images and one comparison. Under trial it is not easy to behave aright, since a candle is not easily kept alight when many envious mouths are puffing at it; and here he brings in Plato, who told a disciple that when men speak ill of thee thou shouldst live so that no one will believe them — good enough advice, he says, but the philosopher did not tell us how to carry it out, whereas the psalm gives the precept in an example: if we would be preserved we must cry to the Preserver. Hold up my goings, he glosses, as a careful driver holds up his horse going down hill; and since we are so weak on our legs through the fall, we need the prayer every hour. Forsaking the enemy’s paths, the psalmist prays to be upheld in God’s, for we cannot keep from evil without keeping to good — if the bushel be not full of wheat it may soon be full of chaff.

On the calling that follows, Keil and Delitzsch make the logic explicit: such a man as he has described himself to be may call upon God, for God hears such and will therefore hear him. Adam Clarke adds that David prayed from a conviction that God would hear but could not be satisfied without an answer, since in a believer’s mind petition and answer should not be separated.
7:
The first word of the seventh verse is disputed before its sense. Charles Ellicott says it means literally to separate, and that from its use for God’s care of Israel in distinction from other nations it acquires the added idea of wonder and miracle, the Greek and Latin rendering it that God should make his mercies appear wonderful. Adam Clarke reports the state of the text: the common reading gives distinguish thy holy ones, but about seventy manuscripts, some ancient editions and the versions read do wonders, and the margin of the verse, he says, is nearer the original than the text. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the sense of separating and turns it into the petition itself, that God would distinguish his mercies and set apart the choicest for this hour of severest affliction. He then divides the request four ways — shew it to my intellect and remove my ignorance, to my heart and revive my gratitude, to my faith and renew my confidence, to my experience and deliver me from my fears. Adam Clarke notes what the psalmist does not do: David was in such danger that he must fall by Saul’s hand unless God worked miracles, yet he lays no claim to miraculous interpositions and expects everything from lovingkindness. John Gill describes that lovingkindness as sovereign, free, everlasting and unchangeable, better than life and passing knowledge, and set upon men and not angels, some and not all.

The apple of the eye is explained by etymology and by anatomy. Charles Ellicott gives the Hebrew literally as little man, daughter of the eye, the mannikin being the reflection seen in the pupil, while daughter is either a contraction of a word meaning cavity or the idiom that expresses relation, as sons of the bow means arrows; and the curious phrase, he notes, is substantially like the Greek and the Latin, even to the gender. Adam Clarke answers with the structure of the head. Take as much care to preserve me by divine influence, he paraphrases, as thou hast taken to preserve my eye by thy providence — having entrenched it deeply in the skull, ramparted it with the forehead and cheek-bones, defended it by the eyebrow, eyelids and eyelashes, and placed it where the hands can best protect it. John Gill makes the same point from the eye’s weakness, since it is put to pain by every little thing that annoys it; and Matthew Henry observes that nature has wonderfully fenced it and teaches us to guard it.

Whose wings shelter him is a smaller question with three answers. Adam Clarke calls it a metaphor taken from the hen and her chickens. Charles Ellicott says the figure of the sheltering wings, common as it is in Hebrew literature, generally refers to the eagle or the vulture, and that it is our English rendering hen which makes our Lord’s use of it more tender. Matthew Henry offers the hen too, and then a third possibility, that the words rather allude to the wings of the cherubim shadowing the mercy-seat.

The last verse of the entry describes the hunt. Adam Clarke reads it as a metaphor taken from huntsmen, who spread themselves around a tract of forest and drive the deer in from every part of the circumference until they are forced into the nets set in some narrow passage, a figure he says is carried on in the verses following. Charles Ellicott works on the adjective, literally with the soul, or better against the life and so deadly, though others take it adverbially and read that the enemies eagerly compass him. John Gill compares the oppressors to wild beasts wasting a field. Matthew Henry reads the petition at two levels, as a prediction of Christ’s preservation through the hardships of his humiliation and as a pattern for Christians committing the keeping of their souls to God.
10:
Whether the enemies are enclosed in fat or in a net divides the entry at once. John Gill keeps the fat and offers a choice of organ: either their eyes, so that they can hardly see out of them, or their hearts, so that they are stupid and senseless; the phrase expressing their wealth and power, by which they were swelled with pride and neither feared God nor regarded man. John Wesley says the same in six words, that they live in splendour and prosperity. Charles Ellicott keeps the fat as a figure only. Literally the words are that they have shut up their fat, which the Greek and Latin render without indicating a meaning; but the proudly of the next clause suggests that fat stands for the conceit of prosperity, and since the verb is active the word mouth should be its object — in their conceit they shut their mouth, and when they do speak, they speak proudly. Adam Clarke removes the fat altogether. Kennicott, Bishop Horsley, Houbigant and others read the clause as saying that they have closed their net upon me, which continues the metaphor of the preceding verse; and the change requires only that a word be brought back from the previous verse and the word for fat be read as the word for net, an emendation of two letters.

The compassing satisfies everyone; the eyes satisfy Clarke in nobody. John Gill says the enemies were so close that the psalmist could not stir a step without their being at his heels, as when Saul followed David to Keilah and the wilderness of Maon; the written text has compassed me and the margin compassed us, and he thinks both right. John Wesley fills in the flight: we go from place to place, to rocks and caves and woods, but wheresoever we go they are at hand, their eyes fixed and couching down upon the earth to watch the fittest opportunity to surprise us. Charles Ellicott calls the text confused. It says literally that they fix their eyes to cast on the earth, which may mean that they fix them on the speaker ready to strike him down; but he prefers a conjecture he calls at once simple and convincing, which brings a word back from the next verse and points it our blood instead of the awkward his likeness: they have set their eyes to shed our blood on the earth.

Then Adam Clarke makes a claim about the whole tradition: all the commentators and critics, he says, have missed the very expressive and elegant metaphor in this clause. He reports what two of them made of it — that the hunters drove the hart into the toils and shot him, and that the attitude described is that of huntsmen taking aim at an animal on the ground — and rejects both: it is the attitude of huntsmen looking for the slot, the track of the hart’s foot, upon the ground.

The lion at the end of the entry is identified and then multiplied. John Gill renders the line as saying that the likeness of him is as a lion, and reports that Kimchi took it of Saul while Aben Ezra applied it to every one of the pursuers, persecuting princes being elsewhere compared to lions for their strength and cruelty. Adam Clarke takes the lion for Saul in his strength, kingly power and fierce rapacity. Keil and Delitzsch read the prayer that follows as an answer to the figure: the foe springs like a lion upon David, and the psalmist asks that the Lord as his defence would cross the lion’s path and intercept him, casting him down so that he lies there harmless with bowed knees. Charles Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has seven names for the lion, and that Milton’s description of Satan stalking round with fiery glare recurs to the reader.
13:
The hunt breaks off into petition. C.H. Spurgeon makes the fervency of the prayer rise with the fury of the attack: God has only to rise from the seat of his patience and the work is done at once. He glosses the second petition as being beforehand with the enemy, outwitting and outrunning him. Adam Clarke keeps the same picture — when the foe rises to spring and tear, let the Lord arise and cast him down. Charles Ellicott presses the Hebrew instead: the word rendered disappoint is rather to go to meet, as a champion goes out to defend another.

The clause naming the wicked as a sword divides them. Charles Ellicott holds that the thought of making the wicked God’s weapon of wrath is arbitrarily introduced by the Authorised Version and quite out of keeping with the context; translate with thy sword, either supplying a preposition or taking the accusative adverbially. Adam Clarke allows both, either the civil power God had entrusted to Saul and which he was now grievously abusing, or a plea to be delivered by God’s own sword. John Wesley keeps the instrument of vengeance and draws a prayer from it: do not punish me with this rod, let me fall into thy hands and not into the hands of men. C.H. Spurgeon rests on the common version — what can a sword do unless a hand wields it? — while granting that most translators read it the other way.

Of the men of the world Adam Clarke is most severe: mortal men of time, temporizers who shift with the times and hold no principle but their own secular interest, whose belly is their god. Their portion is in lives, meaning heritable estates that descend to posterity; and he adds from experience that covetous fathers lay up riches which profligate sons scatter to all the winds of heaven. Charles Ellicott takes the word for world literally as time, from a root meaning that which creeps on, and sees in it an anticipation of the New Testament use; he would also redivide the lines to read that with his treasure God fills their womb, so that they are full of children. John Wesley sharpens the sting: many faithful servants are barren while these are blessed with a numerous posterity. John Gill notes that some, with the Targum, take the verse of another set of men altogether, and those good ones.

The last verse turns on the emphatic I. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to reduce the vision of God’s face to the experience of gracious influences; the parallel clause requires an actual sight of the divine form, of the kind granted to Moses. Adam Clarke says nothing but God can satisfy the wishes of an immortal spirit, and hears an allusion to the creation of Adam, who woke as from sleep and saw his Creator; but he denies that the waking is the resurrection of the body, holding it to be the resurrection of the soul in this life and the regaining of the image Adam lost. John Wesley reads it flatly of rising from the dead, and C.H. Spurgeon of waking at the trumpet: glimpses of glory stay the hunger here, but against that eternal fulness the joys of the worldling are a glowworm to the sun. Charles Ellicott would render likeness as image or appearance, canvasses peace after trouble, health after suffering and the sunlight of grace, but prefers the psalm’s literal night.

Adam Clarke closes with two curiosities: the paraphrase in his old Psalter, which reads the psalm of the passion and resurrection of Christ, as he says Jerome and Augustine did; and a scarce book on hunting, cited by chapter and page, where a woodcut shows a huntsman with his eyes set, bowing to the earth over three slots — offered as proof that the eyes bowed down earlier are a huntsman’s.
